strengths: The paper presents a useful interpretability-security insight: model weights can be fine-tuned to redirect synthetic feature visualizations without adding conspicuous architectural components. This is a meaningful distinction from the cited fooling-circuit attacks.

The gradient-matching and activation-preservation objectives are intuitive and clearly formulated. The toy example effectively illustrates the mechanism, and the idealized one-step construction provides a coherent explanation for its operation.

The MNIST and CIFAR-10 examples demonstrate recognizable target steering. The preservation-weight sweep, 16 model configurations, multiple similarity metrics, and natural-image retrieval analysis provide useful evidence beyond isolated visual examples.

The manuscript candidly reports failures and limitations concerning alternative optimizers and larger images. This transparency is valuable. The benchmark experiments and attributed imagery raise no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The central claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Experiments manipulate a few selected output units and target images; they do not establish manipulation of arbitrary internal neurons or demonstrate concealment of an actual malicious representation during an audit. Representative sampling across neurons and targets, and an explicit audit-evasion experiment, would substantially strengthen the claimed significance.

Preservation of model behavior is insufficiently established. The selected CIFAR-10 attack reduces accuracy from 86.33% to 82.39%, while the targeted unit's AUROC falls from 0.970 to 0.938. Several model-size settings deteriorate considerably more. Aggregate accuracy and a few top-activating images do not establish preservation of the original decision-making process; prediction agreement, per-class performance, and held-out activation changes are needed. The ImageNet performance evaluation covers only 20 classes.

Reliable targeted manipulation under practical visualization procedures remains unproven. In Appendix E, every tested MNIST adjustment removes the target image, and transformation robustness restores the cat visualization on CIFAR-10. Distance from the original visualization measures disruption, which does not establish successful redirection to an arbitrary target. Appendix F shows an initially recognizable ImageNet target that progressively deteriorates during optimization, leaving the larger-scale result incomplete.

The theoretical guarantees apply to an idealized gradient field rather than the fitted network. The empirical gradient loss does not establish the uniform approximation bound assumed in Lemma A.2. That lemma provides a sufficient bound for one-step entry into the landing region, but does not establish convergence to the target: a constant nonzero gradient error shifts the stationary point. Its characterization of the error-dependent radius as necessary or optimal is also unjustified; optimizing the full bound can change the preferred gamma when the error bound is positive.

The empirical study provides little comparison with alternative manipulation objectives and lacks ablations separating the contributions of the slingshot and landing regions. Such controls would clarify whether the particular construction improves the trade-off between target fidelity and preserved performance. The existing parameter and architecture sweeps do not resolve this attribution.

Reproducibility is partial despite the useful appendix details. The manuscript supplies no attack implementation link and omits batch sizes, precise stopping criteria, and clear accounting of independent training runs versus visualization restarts behind the reported variability. The temporary ReLU-to-Softplus substitution also needs its parameters and restoration/evaluation procedure specified. These omissions matter because successful manipulation is sensitive to optimization choices.
